newsitem.title: USA: Discount travel agent scam busted, crooks arrested.
newsitem.headline: Discount travel agent scam busted, crooks arrested.

text.p: Two New York travel agency managers who allegedly sold $1.2 million of phoney discount airline tickets to more than 600 passengers were arrested and arraigned Thursday, the Manhattan District Attorney's Office said.
The brothers, Asim Chaughtai and Atif Ismail, were preparing to flee to Pakistan Friday night when they were caught by New York City police.

The scam was discovered when passengers showed up at airports throughout the country and were told that their tickets, issued by Amsag Travel Corp. on Madison Avenue in New York City, were "stolen" and invalid.
While some airlines honoured the tickets, many passengers were left stranded. Many have still not been used, a spokesman at the Manhattan District Attorney's office said.
Most of the tickets -- paid for in cash, by check or credit card -- were for trans-Atlantic flights on international carriers.

The tickets were sold from around Oct. 1 through Dec. 4 by Chaughtai, 33, and Ismail, 30, who became managers of Amsag in March, court papers show. The brothers allegedly failed to report ticket sales to the Airline Reporting Corp., an industry clearinghouse that processes such transactions, and stole the money.

Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau filed grand larceny charges against the brothers, who live in Huntington Station in Long Island, N.Y., alleging a felony that carries a sentence of up to 25 years in prison.
Morgenthau's office began a criminal investigation two weeks ago after it was informed of the scam -- known in the industry as a "bust out" -- by the Airline Reporting Corp., based in Arlington, Va.
The office spokesman declined to comment on the owners of Amsag, which closed on Dec. 9 after 20 years in business.
Aamir Zakaria, a victim of the scam, said American Airlines confiscated his tickets to Pakistan when he showed up with his wife at the airport in Nashville, Tenn., last week.

"When we asked how long they knew about (the scam), they said since Dec. 4," he said. "If they'd known a week in advance, why wait till we showed up with our bags packed before telling us there's a problem? They could have put an announcement in the paper."
A spokeswoman for AMR Corp., parent of American Airlines, had no immediate comment.
Steve Loucks, spokesman for the American Society of Travel Agents, with 33,000 members nationwide, said this was the first time he has come across such a scam.
The society has received several complaints since Dec. 9.
"We try through our consumer affairs department to resolve all those problems," Loucks said. "We can't guarantee action because we are only a trade organisation ..."
